## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Three goals for today. First, you learn how to navigate the R Studio interface
and how to issue basic commands to R. Second, we explore the three concepts that
everything else in R builds on: objects, functions, and assignments. Third, we
learn how to use existing functions and how to write our own.

As in the first session, the slides are deliberately lean — the full wording
lives here in the speaker notes and can be read separately as a script.

## Slide 4 · After starting R Studio

When you start R Studio for the first time, you will see something like this.
Two panes: on the left the console, where R greets you with its version number
and a `>` prompt, and on the right the environment pane at the top and the
files pane at the bottom.

Do not worry about the details yet — we will go through the individual elements
in a moment.

## Slide 5 · Some general settings

As a first step I recommend you adjust some general settings. Go to R Studio,
then Settings, then General, and make sure that the box "Restore .RData into
workspace at startup" is unchecked, and that "Save workspace to .RData on exit"
is set to "Never".

Why does this matter so much? If R restores your old workspace, you keep working
with objects that are no longer created by your current script. Your analysis
then appears to work on your machine, but nowhere else — and not even on your
own machine after a restart. The whole point of scripting is that the script
reproduces the result from scratch. Leftover objects in the workspace are the
single most common reason why that silently stops being true.

## Slide 6 · Working with a script

Create a new script, and you will see R Studio in the way you will work with it
most of the time: now there are four panes rather than two, because the script
editor has opened in the upper left.

This is the layout you should get used to. You write your commands in the
script, not in the console — the script is the thing that is saved, versioned
and handed in.

## Slide 7 · The most important elements

The four panes, and what they are for.

The script editor, upper left: a 'fancy' text editor to write and modify R
files. The run button at the top of it executes the marked part of the script in
the console.

The console, lower left: used to issue commands to the computer directly.

The environment, upper right: an overview of all objects you have defined so
far.

The files pane, lower right: the files in your current project, that is, your
working directory.

We will learn about environments, projects and working directories in more
detail later — for today, just remember where things are.

## Slide 9 · Issuing commands

Now let us practise how to issue commands to R. The simplest commands are
arithmetic ones — R works as a calculator out of the box.

All the practical steps, and quite a bit of additional information, are
summarised in the section "Issue commands to your computer" of the tutorial
"First Steps in R" on the course page. Read it after the session; everything we
do here is written up there in more detail.

## Slide 10 · Intermediate task

Sit together in groups of two or three and execute these four computations via
the console.

The point of the last one is the bracketing: you need to write
`(8**2 + 5**4) / 3`. If you forget the brackets, R divides only the second
summand by three and returns a different — but perfectly valid-looking — number.
That is the first lesson about programming: the computer does what you write,
not what you mean.

## Slide 12 · Two slogans

John Chambers, one of the creators of the S language from which R descends, put
it in two slogans: everything that exists is an object, and everything that
happens is a function call.

Every number, every function, every letter — whatever there is — is an object
that is stored somewhere in the physical memory of your computer. And whenever
we tell our computer to do something via R, we are effectively calling a
function.

## Slide 13 · `2 + 3` refers to three objects

Take the operation `2 + 3`. It already refers to three objects: the numbers 2
and 3, and the function `+`, which performs the addition. Executing it produces
yet another object, the number 5.

This sounds pedantic, but it pays off: once you accept that the plus sign is a
function and the result is an object, nothing in R will surprise you
structurally later on.

## Slide 14 · Assignments

What if we wanted to keep the result of a computation for further use?

When you type `2 + 3`, the result is created after the addition has been
executed and stored somewhere in your computer memory. Since it is impossible to
remember that precise location, the way to go is to give the result a name, and
then later call it by this name.

This process of binding an object to a name is called an assignment. It is done
by the function `assign()`: the name `int_results` is now bound to the result of
`2 + 3`.

## Slide 15 · The environment shows your names

You can now call the result by its name: typing `int_results` returns 5.

And you see all the names currently given in the upper right pane of R Studio.
Before the assignment the environment is empty; afterwards it lists
`int_results` with the value 5. Whenever you are unsure whether an object really
exists, or what it currently contains, this is the pane to look at.

## Slide 16 · Shortcuts, names, and removal

Since assignments happen frequently, there is a shortcut to using `assign()`:
the arrow operator. `int_result <- 2 + 3` does exactly the same as
`assign("int_result", 2 + 3)`, and it is what you will see in practically all R
code. Do learn the keyboard shortcut for it — on a Mac, Option and minus.

Not all names are allowed; the tutorial reading lists the rules.

You can remove an assignment by calling the function `rm()` on the name. After
`rm(x)`, calling `x` gives you an error: the name no longer points to anything.

## Slide 17 · What about many assignments?

One object can have many names, but each name can only point to one single
object. If you assign 2 to `a` and then assign 4 to `a`, the name `a` now refers
to 4 — the previous binding is simply gone, without any warning.

Be aware not to overwrite important pre-defined assignments. If you name your
own object `mean`, you have a problem the next time you want to compute a mean.

In the worst case, remove all assignments and restart R — on a Mac with Shift,
Command and zero. This is not a failure; restarting a session frequently is a
good habit, because it proves your script still works from a clean slate.

## Slide 18 · Tasks

Get together again in groups of two or three and compute this chain problem,
assigning a name to each intermediate result. The point is that you can use a
name on the right-hand side of the next assignment: `b <- 5 * a / 2` works
because `a` already exists.

The second question is deliberate: find out what happens if you call a name that
has not been assigned to an object before. You will get the "object not found"
error from the previous slide — and recognising that error message quickly is
genuinely useful.

## Slide 20 · What a function is

A function is an algorithm which takes an input, applies a routine, and returns
an output.

The function `log()`, for instance, computes the logarithm of a number: you give
it the number 2, it applies the logarithm routine, and returns 0.6931472.

Functions usually have names that we can use to call them, and there are two
main ways to call a function: the prefix and the infix form.

## Slide 21 · Calling functions: prefix and infix

The most common form is the prefix form: first the name of the function, then
open brackets, then the arguments separated by commas, then closed brackets. The
arguments usually include the input.

Alternatively we might use the infix form, where the function name is written
between the arguments — as in `2 + 3`. This is most common for mathematical
operations. The further readings say more about it.

## Slide 22 · Two types of arguments

There are two different types of arguments: mandatory arguments and optional
arguments.

Mandatory arguments usually represent the function input. Optional arguments
allow you to specify details on how the function routine should be executed.

The practical difference: while mandatory arguments can be specified via their
name, optional arguments usually must be specified via their name. Let us look
at this with the example of `mean()`.

## Slide 23 · Mandatory arguments

We first use the function `c()` — which stands for concatenate — to create a
vector of numbers, and assign it the name `t_vec`.

We then want to use `mean()` to compute the mean of this set of numbers, so we
write `mean(t_vec)`.

The first, mandatory argument of `mean()` is called `x` and means the set of
which the mean should be computed. Being a mandatory argument, we can specify it
by name — `mean(x = t_vec)` — but we do not need to. Both calls do exactly the
same thing.

## Slide 24 · Optional arguments

Among others, `mean()` also accepts an optional argument called `na.rm`. It
specifies how `mean()` should deal with missing values in the original input. If
`na.rm` equals TRUE, then missing values — written `NA` in R — are removed
before the mean gets computed. If it equals FALSE, they are not.

We set this value by writing the name of the optional argument followed by an
equals sign and the value.

Now add a missing value to our original vector and test how the three
applications of `mean()` differ. Two of them return `NA`, one returns 2.5 — and
you should be able to say which and why before you run it.

## Slide 25 · Defaults, Tab, and `help()`

As all optional arguments, `na.rm` has a default value that is chosen if you do
not set another value explicitly. For `mean()` that default is FALSE — which
explains the result of the plain `mean(t_vec)` call on the previous slide.

How do you know whether there are optional arguments, what their defaults are,
or what the names of the arguments are? Two ways. Press the Tab key after having
written the open bracket, and R Studio shows you the arguments. Or call the
function `help()` — here, `help(mean)` — which opens the documentation in the
lower right pane.

Getting comfortable with the help pages early pays off enormously. They are
terse, but they are complete.

## Slide 26 · Function calls — practice

Define a vector with the elements minus two, two, four, six, nine and NA, then
apply these four functions and work out what each of them is doing.

`is.na()` and `anyNA()` differ in an instructive way: one returns a vector of
TRUE/FALSE values, the other a single TRUE or FALSE.

The last question is the interesting one. `var()` computes the sample variance,
dividing by n minus one. To get the population variance you have to multiply by
(n-1)/n yourself. The lesson is that you must always check what a statistical
function actually computes — the name alone does not tell you.

## Slide 27 · Defining your own functions

Knowing how to define your own functions is important for two reasons. First,
defining own functions is super useful and often recommendable. Second, it
allows us to better understand how functions work in general.

And there is a nice circularity to it: we define a new function via the function
`function()`.

## Slide 28 · The anatomy of a function

Let us go through the anatomy of a function definition.

First the name of the new function and the assignment operator — a function
definition is an assignment like any other, which is why the arrow appears here.

Then `function()` with the arguments of the new function in brackets: here two
catheti.

Then the function body in curly braces: the routine the function should apply to
the input. Here we square both catheti, add them, and take the square root.

Finally `return()`, specifying what the function returns as its output.

The crucial point is the last one: all associations inside the body only exist
within the function. After calling `pythagoras(3, 4)`, there is no object called
`hypo_squared` in your environment. That is a feature, not a limitation — it is
what keeps functions from interfering with the rest of your code.

## Slide 29 · Short practice

Write a function that takes two mandatory arguments, x1 and x2, and returns the
result of this equation. Use the pythagoras function from the previous slide as
your template.

If someone finishes early: ask them what the function returns if you call it
with a vector instead of a single number, and why.

## Slide 30 · Final remarks about functions

There are many reasons to use functions. Code becomes more concise and
transparent. Functions help to structure your code. And they facilitate
debugging and help avoid incidental mistakes — if a computation exists exactly
once, it can also be wrong only in exactly one place.

Before writing a function in daily life, check via a search engine whether it
has not already been written. For anything more complicated, it is usually a
good idea to sketch your ideas with pen and paper and then implement them.

And always document your functions. The readings contain a manual on how to do
that.

## Slide 31 · Let's practice!

Go together in pairs; one of you is the driver, the other the navigator. Only
the driver writes code, the navigator tells them what to do. Swap roles halfway
if you like.

After fifteen minutes, sit together with another team, explain your solutions
and discuss common problems. Then we have a short general feedback round in the
plenum.

The task is to write a function that takes a set of numbers as an input and
normalises them into the range of zero and one. The functions `min()` and
`max()` come in handy.

Watch for the case where all values are identical — then the denominator is
zero. Nobody needs to solve that today, but it is a good thing to notice.

## Slide 32 · Summary

So, you made your first big steps into the R programming world.

We checked out the main elements of the R Studio interface. We learned about how
to issue commands to the computer. We learned that everything in R that exists
is an object, and everything that happens is a function call. We learned how to
associate objects with names. And we learned how to call and define functions.

This was a lot for one session. It is a good idea to take your time to digest
and repeat these topics rather than rushing ahead.

## Slide 33 · Outlook

Next session we will learn about the different types of objects you can
encounter in R, and how to automate tasks with loops and conditionals. Then we
are finished with the general introduction and move on to data visualisation.
